item.title: NY Fed's John Williams flags need to gather more information on inflation risks before rate decisions
item.description: Federal Reserve officials John Williams and Alberto Musalem have flagged persistent inflation risks, with rapid AI infrastructure investment potentially adding to price pressures. Williams backed the need for more economic data before determining monetary policy, while Musalem warned that policymakers must address current inflation rather than wait for future AI-driven productivity gains.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve officials are weighing the inflationary risks from strong economic activity and the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, even as they signal the need for more data before determining the next steps on interest rates, Bloomberg reported.For live updates on US Markets, click here New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remained too high, although other indicators were not yet pointing to broader concerns. Speaking at an event hosted by the European Central Bank in Frankfurt on Friday, he backed the Fed's position that policymakers should gather more information before deciding the appropriate course for monetary policy. Inflation is absolutely too high, Williams said, while noting that wage growth remained consistent with the central bank's 2% inflation target and inflation expectations were well anchored.Fed weighs inflation against economic resilienceWilliams said monetary policy had an important role in preventing temporary price shocks from spreading into broader or more persistent inflation.Also Read: Federal Reserve rate hike bets strengthen as US jobs growth beats estimates Our FOMC statement last meeting, I think, captures correctly that this is an appropriate time to accumulate more information to help us determine what the appropriate stance of policy is to make make sure we achieve a timely return to our 2% target, he said, according to the Bloomberg report.The Fed held interest rates steady at its previous meeting after raising its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in September to a range of 3.75%-4%. Policymakers have since emphasised the need for additional information while keeping the possibility of further rate increases open, Bloomberg reported.The central bank's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier. Underlying inflation measures that exclude food and energy also increased. Meanwhile, the US economy expanded at its fastest pace in a year in the quarter ended September.AI infrastructure raises fresh inflation concernsSeparately, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem warned that the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure could add to near-term inflationary pressures, Bloomberg reported. When I look at inflation, excess inflation today, it’s coming both from negative supply shocks related to the Middle East and demand forces coming related to the AI build, Musalem said.While acknowledging AI's potential to improve productivity over time, he cautioned against shaping current monetary policy around benefits that may take years to materialise. We need to make monetary policy for the economy of the day, he said. We cannot make monetary policy for the economy as it may be five years from now. item.title: Federal Reserve rate hike bets strengthen as US jobs growth beats estimates
item.description: Stronger than expected US jobs growth has revived expectations of a December Federal Reserve rate hike, with employers adding 165,000 jobs in October against estimates of 65,000. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, while markets raised the probability of a quarter point hike to 85% and brought forward expectations of another increase.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: The Federal Reserve's case for another interest rate hike in December has gained momentum after stronger than expected US employment data reinforced signs of economic resilience, shifting attention back to persistent inflation from concerns over a potential AI driven slowdown, Reuters reported.US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than double the 65,000 expected by economists, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The unemployment rate also edged down to 4.1%, suggesting the labour market remains firm despite concerns over the economic outlook.For live updates on US Markets, click here Following the report, markets priced in an 85% probability of a quarter point rate increase at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, up from around 75% before the data release. Traders also brought forward expectations of another rate increase to April from June, Reuters reported.Strong jobs data reinforce Fed's hawkish outlookThe employment figures strengthen the argument for further monetary tightening as the Fed continues to battle inflation, which has remained above its 2% target for more than five years.Also Read: Nasdaq rebounds as chip stocks recover from steep losses, rate fears persist This is a very strong labor market report on the heels of solid GDP and consumer spending data last week, reinforcing the economy’s positive momentum, Fitch Ratings analyst Olu Sonola wrote after the release.While acknowledging the risks posed by recent AI related concerns, Sonola said the economy remained on firm footing and that labour market resilience was pushing the policy debate towards a December rate hike, Reuters reported.Raymond James analysts also expect the central bank to raise rates next month. For the Federal Reserve, this should allow them to concentrate on the inflation side of their mandate, the analysts wrote. We expect the Fed to increase the federal funds rate by 25 basis points in December. AI concerns had clouded rate outlookExpectations of another rate increase had weakened after Democrats' midterm election gains raised concerns about tighter regulation of AI and data centre construction.The prospect of slower AI investment had fuelled worries about weaker economic growth and easing inflationary pressures, reducing the urgency for further monetary tightening.However, Friday's employment report has renewed expectations that the Fed will prioritise inflation control as it assesses the strength of the US economy.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)
